stories.title: Ndaje
stories.teaser: A Guaraní–Spanish court interpreter in Asunción hears a tiny word missing from a police transcript, and an arson trial in Paraguay's sugar-cane country suddenly hinges on the difference between seeing and hearing.
lines: «Quien faltare a la verdad en su declaración incurrirá en falso testimonio.» Perla Benítez había oído esa advertencia tantas veces, en castellano y en guaraní, que a veces la recitaba en sueños, con la misma cadencia de misa con que la leían los actuarios del Palacio de Justicia de Asunción. Llevaba veinte años como intérprete jurada y sabía que nadie, salvo los abogados viejos, conjugaba ya aquel futuro de subjuntivo que sobrevivía en los códigos como un mueble de la abuela: pesado, inútil para la vida diaria e imposible de tirar. En la tapa de su cuaderno de notas había escrito, con letra de colegiala, una sola regla: las palabras chicas pesan más que las grandes.

“Whoever shall fail to tell the truth in their testimony shall be guilty of perjury.” Perla Benítez had heard that warning so many times, in Spanish and in Guaraní, that she sometimes recited it in her sleep, with the same churchy cadence the clerks of Asunción’s Palace of Justice used when they read it out. She had been a sworn interpreter for twenty years and knew that nobody, except old lawyers, still conjugated that future subjunctive, which survived in the legal codes like a piece of a grandmother’s furniture: heavy, useless in daily life and impossible to throw away. On the cover of her notebook she had written, in a schoolgirl’s hand, a single rule: small words weigh more than big ones.

El expediente le llegó un viernes de agosto, a última hora, porque el intérprete asignado estaba internado con neumonía y el juicio oral no podía postergarse otra vez. Derlis Cañete, de veintiséis años, cañero de una compañía del departamento de Paraguarí, estaba acusado de haber provocado el incendio intencional que, una noche de viento norte, arrasó el cañaveral de su vecino, Nicasio Leguizamón, y de paso los surcos de otras tres familias. Los dos hombres llevaban años enfrentados por un lindero: medio metro de alambrado corrido que ninguno estaba dispuesto a perdonar. Derlis juraba haber pasado la noche del fuego en un baile de la compañía vecina, pero nadie recordaba haberlo visto bailar. Nicasio, dueño del único trapiche de la zona, había declarado ante la policía que esa semana la molienda estaba parada, de modo que el fuego, concluía el acta, solo podía haber venido de afuera.

The case file reached her late on a Friday in August, because the interpreter originally assigned was in hospital with pneumonia and the trial could not be postponed again. Derlis Cañete, twenty-six, a cane grower from a rural community in the department of Paraguarí, was accused of having started the deliberate fire that, on a night of hot north wind, had destroyed the cane field of his neighbour, Nicasio Leguizamón, and the rows of three other families along with it. The two men had been at odds for years over a property line: half a metre of moved fence that neither of them was willing to forgive. Derlis swore he had spent the night of the fire at a dance in the neighbouring community, but nobody remembered seeing him dance. Nicasio, owner of the only sugar-cane mill in the area, had told the police that the mill had been idle that week, so the fire, the report concluded, could only have come from outside.

Toda la acusación descansaba en una sola prueba testimonial: la de ña Gumersinda Ozorio, de ochenta y un años, que vivía entre los dos campos y no hablaba una palabra de castellano. En la versión policial, firmada al pie por un agente que «declara conocer suficientemente el idioma guaraní», la anciana afirmaba: «Vi a Derlis al borde de la chacra, con un bidón en la mano». Esa noche, en su departamento de Sajonia, con los auriculares puestos y el ventilador peleando contra un agosto que no parecía invierno, Perla escuchó la grabación original. Ahí estaba, metida entre el nombre y el verbo, breve como un carraspeo: «Derlis ndaje oĩ va'ekue kokue rembe'ýpe, peteĩ bidón ipópe». No decía «lo vi». Decía, como mucho, «dicen que estaba».

The whole prosecution rested on a single piece of witness evidence: that of ña Gumersinda Ozorio, eighty-one, who lived between the two fields and did not speak a word of Spanish. In the police version, signed at the bottom by an officer who “states that he has a sufficient command of the Guaraní language”, the old woman said: “I saw Derlis at the edge of the field, with a jerrycan in his hand.” That night, in her flat in Sajonia, with her headphones on and the fan battling an August that did not feel like winter, Perla listened to the original recording. There it was, tucked between the name and the verb, as short as someone clearing their throat: “Derlis ndaje oĩ va'ekue kokue rembe'ýpe, peteĩ bidón ipópe.” It did not say “I saw him.” At most, it said “they say he was there.”

Había algo más. Al final de la grabación, cuando el agente ya guardaba sus papeles, ña Gumersinda había añadido una frase que la transcripción despachaba entre corchetes como «comentarios irrelevantes de la testigo». Perla la escuchó cuatro veces y la anotó en el margen, con un signo de pregunta: esa noche, decía la anciana, toda la compañía olía a miel quemada. Después redactó, en el lenguaje que el oficio exigía, una nota para el tribunal: «Por la presente, la abajo firmante, intérprete jurada, pone en conocimiento de este Tribunal que la versión obrante en autos omite una partícula reportativa, en virtud de lo cual solicita que la traducción sea rectificada y, si así no se hiciere, que se deje constancia de la omisión en el acta».

There was something else. At the end of the recording, when the officer was already putting his papers away, ña Gumersinda had added a sentence that the transcript dismissed in square brackets as “irrelevant remarks by the witness”. Perla listened to it four times and wrote it in the margin, with a question mark: that night, the old woman said, the whole community smelled of burnt cane syrup. Then she drafted, in the language her profession demanded, a note to the court: “The undersigned, a sworn interpreter, hereby informs this Court that the version on file omits a reportative particle, by virtue of which she requests that the translation be corrected and, should this not be done, that the omission be recorded in the minutes.”

El lunes por la mañana, en el pasillo, el fiscal Osmar Villalba leyó la nota sin quitarse los anteojos y se la devolvió doblada en cuatro. —¿Me está diciendo que voy a perder un juicio por una palabrita, señora? —Le estoy diciendo que su testigo no vio nada. Habla por boca de ganso, fiscal: repite lo que le contaron. —Cuando el río suena, piedras trae. Si toda la compañía dice que fue Derlis, por algo será. —Entonces cite al río a declarar —contestó Perla—, porque esta señora, que yo sepa, no lo vio. Villalba sonrió sin ganas. Era un hombre honesto, decían en el Palacio, y precisamente por eso detestaba que le movieran el piso a cinco minutos de una audiencia.

On Monday morning, in the corridor, prosecutor Osmar Villalba read the note without taking off his glasses and handed it back to her folded in four.
“Are you telling me I’m going to lose a trial over one little word, madam?”
“I’m telling you your witness didn’t see anything. She’s just parroting, prosecutor: she repeats what she was told.”
“Where there’s smoke, there’s fire. If the whole community says it was Derlis, there must be a reason.”
“Then summon the smoke to testify,” Perla replied, “because this lady, as far as I know, didn’t see him.”
Villalba gave a reluctant smile. He was an honest man, people said at the Palace, and that was precisely why he hated having the ground pulled from under him five minutes before a hearing.

La sala tenía paneles de madera oscura, ventiladores de techo que giraban con pereza y, detrás del estrado, la bandera tricolor. Presidía el tribunal la jueza Casilda Duarte, famosa por no levantar nunca la voz ni la vista del expediente. En la primera fila, Nicasio Leguizamón, que a primera hora había jurado que esa semana su trapiche no había molido una sola caña, se abanicaba con el sombrero. En un panel, una fotografía ampliada mostraba el cañaveral quemado: una mancha negra que se abría en abanico desde la esquina más alejada del camino. Ña Gumersinda entró del brazo de una nieta, con un vestido floreado y un rosario enroscado en la muñeca. Perla tuvo que prestar juramento de traducir fielmente; prestado el juramento, se acercó a la anciana. —Mba'éichapa, ña Gumersinda. —Iporã, mi hija. Vení-na un ratito, sentate conmigo.

The courtroom had dark wood panelling, ceiling fans turning lazily and, behind the bench, the red, white and blue flag. Presiding over the court was Judge Casilda Duarte, famous for never raising her voice or her eyes from the case file. In the front row, Nicasio Leguizamón, who had sworn first thing that morning that his mill had not crushed a single cane that week, was fanning himself with his hat. On a board, an enlarged photograph showed the burnt cane field: a black stain that opened out like a fan from the corner farthest from the road. Ña Gumersinda came in on a granddaughter’s arm, wearing a flowered dress, a rosary wound round her wrist. Perla had to take an oath to interpret faithfully; once sworn in, she went over to the old woman.
“Mba'éichapa, ña Gumersinda. How are you?”
“Fine, dear. Come here a moment, won’t you, sit with me.”

Leída el acta de la declaración policial, la presidenta preguntó a la testigo si la ratificaba. Perla levantó la mano antes de traducir.
—Con la venia del tribunal: la versión que acaba de leerse no corresponde a la grabación. La testigo no dijo «lo vi». Dijo «ndaje», que en guaraní indica que uno no da fe de lo que cuenta, sino que lo repite. Es nuestro «dicen que».
El fiscal objetó que a la intérprete no le correspondía opinar sobre la prueba. Rosalba Insfrán, la defensora pública, pidió entonces que se le preguntara directamente a la testigo cómo sabía lo que sabía. La jueza Duarte consultó con sus colegas en un murmullo y, por primera vez en la mañana, levantó la vista.
—Proceda.

Once the record of the police statement had been read, the presiding judge asked the witness whether she confirmed it. Perla raised her hand before interpreting.
“With the court’s permission: the version that has just been read does not match the recording. The witness did not say ‘I saw him.’ She said ‘ndaje’, which in Guaraní shows that the speaker isn’t vouching for what she reports, only repeating it. It’s our ‘they say that’.”
The prosecutor objected that it was not the interpreter’s place to comment on the evidence. Rosalba Insfrán, the public defender, then asked that the witness be asked directly how she knew what she knew. Judge Duarte conferred with her colleagues in a murmur and, for the first time that morning, looked up.
“Go ahead.”

Perla se volvió hacia la anciana y le habló en el jopará de las cocinas y los colectivos, esa mezcla de guaraní y castellano que en el Paraguay casi nadie siente como mezcla: —Che ra'a, ¿vos lo viste o te contaron? Ña Gumersinda se rió con toda la boca. —¿Con qué ojos, mi hija? De noche ya no veo ni mi mano. Nicasio he'i chéve. Nicasio me dijo, a la mañana, cuando fui a comprarle miel al trapiche. Una vez traducida la frase, nadie dijo nada. Solo se oían los ventiladores. El acusado levantó la cabeza por primera vez, y Perla vio en su cara algo peor que el miedo: el asombro de quien descubre que lo habían juzgado de boca en boca mucho antes que en ningún tribunal.

Perla turned to the old woman and spoke to her in the jopará of kitchens and buses, that blend of Guaraní and Spanish that hardly anyone in Paraguay feels to be a blend:
“Che ra'a, my dear, did you see him or did someone tell you?”
Ña Gumersinda laughed with her whole mouth.
“With what eyes, dear? At night I can’t even see my own hand. Nicasio he'i chéve. Nicasio told me, in the morning, when I went to buy syrup from him at the mill.”
Once the sentence had been interpreted, nobody said anything. All you could hear were the fans. The defendant raised his head for the first time, and Perla saw something worse than fear in his face: the astonishment of a man who discovers he had been tried by word of mouth long before any court.

A Villalba hay que reconocerle que no se sentó. Pidió permiso para una última pregunta y, para sorpresa de Perla, sacó de la carpeta la nota doblada en cuatro: había leído también el margen. ¿Había sentido la testigo algún olor aquella noche? La respuesta llegó larga, mezclada, con un «luego» al final que Perla tradujo sin traducir, porque en boca paraguaya no significa «después» sino «así es, nomás»: la compañía entera olía a miel quemada, porque Nicasio cocinaba de noche, que de día el calor no deja trabajar, y esa semana había molido hasta tarde. Según el acta, esa misma semana el trapiche había estado parado. El fiscal se quedó mirando la fotografía del panel. La mancha negra se abría desde la esquina más alejada del camino, justo la que daba a la chimenea del trapiche.

Credit where it’s due: Villalba did not sit down. He asked permission for one last question and, to Perla’s surprise, took the note folded in four out of his folder: he had read the margin too. Had the witness noticed any smell that night? The answer came out long and mixed, with a “luego” at the end that Perla interpreted without translating, because in a Paraguayan mouth it doesn’t mean “later” but “that’s just how it is”: the whole community smelled of burnt syrup, because Nicasio boiled it at night, since the daytime heat makes work impossible, and that week he had been crushing cane until late. According to the report, the mill had been idle that very week. The prosecutor stood staring at the photograph on the board. The black stain opened out from the corner farthest from the road, precisely the one that faced the mill’s chimney.

Terminada la audiencia, el fiscal alcanzó a Perla en la escalera. —¿Usted pondría las manos en el fuego por ese muchacho? —Yo no pongo las manos en el fuego por nadie, fiscal. Las pongo en las palabras. A la semana siguiente, a pedido del propio Villalba, el tribunal ordenó una inspección en el lugar, y Perla viajó a Paraguarí en una camioneta del Ministerio Público. Entre los rastrojos negros, un peón del trapiche llamado Toribio, que solo hablaba guaraní y retorcía el sombrero entre las manos, contó lo que nadie le había preguntado: que esa noche la chimenea escupía chispas como fuegos artificiales, que soplaba un norte caliente y que el patrón, a la mañana, le había ordenado decir, si alguien preguntaba, que el trapiche estaba parado. —¡Había sido cierto lo de la miel! —se le escapó a Perla.

Once the hearing was over, the prosecutor caught up with Perla on the stairs.
“Would you vouch for that young man, hand on heart?”
“I don’t vouch for anyone, prosecutor. I vouch for words.”
The following week, at Villalba’s own request, the court ordered an on-site inspection, and Perla travelled to Paraguarí in a Public Prosecutor’s Office pickup truck. Among the blackened stubble, a mill hand called Toribio, who spoke only Guaraní and kept twisting his hat in his hands, told them what nobody had asked him: that on that night the chimney was spitting sparks like fireworks, that a hot north wind was blowing, and that in the morning the boss had ordered him to say, if anyone asked, that the mill had been idle.
“So that business with the syrup was true!” Perla blurted out.

Lo demás lo reconstruyó la fiscalía en pocos días. Si el fuego había salido del trapiche, Nicasio tendría que responder ante las tres familias cuyos surcos se habían quemado con los suyos; si lo había encendido un vecino con un bidón, Nicasio era una víctima más. Esa misma mañana, mientras vendía miel, empezó a decir que había sido Derlis, y el rumor hizo el resto: de la cocina de ña Gumersinda a la despensa, de la despensa a la parada del colectivo y de ahí, convertido en certeza, al acta policial. Una colega colombiana le había dicho una vez a Perla que en su tierra a eso lo llamaban un dizque: dizque lo vieron con un bidón, dizque fue él. Según parece, nadie lo vio nunca; todos lo habían oído. En su alegato final, Villalba hizo algo que en el Palacio no se veía todos los días: pidió la absolución. —Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho, señorías, y en esta causa no hubo hecho. Hubo dicho.

The prosecution reconstructed the rest in a few days. If the fire had come from the mill, Nicasio would have to answer to the three families whose rows had burned along with his; if a neighbour with a jerrycan had started it, Nicasio was just one more victim. That same morning, while he was selling syrup, he began saying that it had been Derlis, and the rumour did the rest: from ña Gumersinda’s kitchen to the corner shop, from the corner shop to the bus stop and from there, turned into certainty, into the police report. A Colombian colleague had once told Perla that back home they called that a dizque: supposedly they saw him with a jerrycan, supposedly it was him. As far as anyone could tell, nobody had ever seen it; everybody had heard it. In his closing argument, Villalba did something you didn’t see every day at the Palace: he asked for an acquittal.
“Saying is one thing and doing is another, your honours, and in this case there was no doing. There was only saying.”

El tribunal resolvió por unanimidad absolver a Derlis Cañete y remitió los antecedentes a la fiscalía para que investigara si Nicasio había incurrido en falso testimonio al jurar que su trapiche estaba parado. Absuelto el muchacho, la sala se vació en pocos minutos. En la vereda, Derlis le dio la mano a Perla sin saber muy bien qué decirle y al final dijo «aguyje», gracias, como se lo habría dicho a su abuela. En el pasillo, dos funcionarias comentaban ya, a media voz, que el del trapiche iba a terminar preso, ndaje, y Perla sonrió: el rumor había cambiado de dirección, no de naturaleza.

The court unanimously decided to acquit Derlis Cañete and referred the case back to the prosecution to investigate whether Nicasio had committed perjury when he swore that his mill was idle. Once the young man had been acquitted, the courtroom emptied in a few minutes. On the pavement, Derlis shook Perla’s hand without really knowing what to say to her, and in the end he said “aguyje”, thank you, as he would have said it to his grandmother. In the corridor, two court employees were already saying, under their breath, that the mill owner was going to end up in jail, so they say, and Perla smiled: the rumour had changed direction, not its nature.

Esa noche, ya en Sajonia, se preparó un tereré aunque no hacía calor y pensó en ña Gumersinda, que no había mentido en ningún momento: había dicho ndaje, con toda honradez, y fueron otros los que se tragaron la palabra por el camino. Después abrió el cuaderno y, debajo de la regla de las palabras chicas, escribió el refrán con que su madre la había despedido cuando se fue a estudiar a Asunción, con una valija de cartón y dos idiomas: «Adonde fueres, haz lo que vieres». Lo pensó un momento, mordiendo el lápiz como a los veinte años, y añadió con su letra de colegiala, en el mismo futuro de subjuntivo que nadie usaba ya: «y di lo que oyeres, pero di que lo oíste».

That night, back in Sajonia, she made herself a tereré even though it wasn’t hot and thought about ña Gumersinda, who had not lied at any point: she had said ndaje, in all honesty, and it was others who had swallowed the word along the way. Then she opened her notebook and, under the rule about small words, wrote down the proverb her mother had sent her off with when she left to study in Asunción, with a cardboard suitcase and two languages: “When in Rome, do as the Romans do.” She thought for a moment, chewing her pencil as she had at twenty, and added in her schoolgirl’s hand, in the same future subjunctive that nobody used anymore: “and repeat what you hear, but say that you heard it.”
vocab: oral trial (public trial with live testimony)
official record, minutes (of a hearing or statement)
to take an oath, be sworn in
stubble (left in a field after harvest or fire)

quiz.q: Según su declaración, ¿qué pasaba con el trapiche de Nicasio la semana del incendio?
options: Que lo había alquilado a Derlis
Que la chimenea estaba rota desde el invierno
Que estaba parado y no molía caña
Que funcionaba día y noche sin descanso

quiz.q: ¿Por qué la palabra ndaje cambia el valor de la declaración de ña Gumersinda?
options: Porque demuestra que la anciana mintió a la policía
Porque indica que ella repetía lo que otros decían, no lo que vio
Porque en guaraní es una forma de jurar que algo es verdad
Porque prueba que Derlis estaba en el baile

quiz.q: ¿Qué quiere decir Perla con «Yo no pongo las manos en el fuego por nadie, fiscal. Las pongo en las palabras»?
options: Que está segura de que Derlis es inocente
Que el resultado del juicio le resulta indiferente
Que teme que la acusen de falso testimonio
Que su lealtad es con la exactitud de lo dicho, no con las personas

quiz.q: En el texto, el «alegato» final de Villalba es…
options: su exposición final ante el tribunal, en la que pide la absolución
una queja formal contra la intérprete
el acta de la declaración policial
el juramento que prestan los testigos

quiz.q: ¿Qué detalle, despachado como «irrelevante» en la transcripción policial, ayuda a resolver el caso?
options: El rosario que ña Gumersinda llevaba en la muñeca
El baile en la compañía vecina
El olor a miel quemada que había esa noche
La camisa prestada de Derlis

stories.prompt: Imagine you are Perla writing a short formal report to the court after the trial. In Spanish (6-8 sentences), explain what went wrong with the police translation and what should be done in future cases. Use at least two absolute constructions (leída el acta..., una vez...), one formula with the future subjunctive (quien..., si así no se hiciere...) and mark the source of each piece of information (según..., dicen que..., había sido...). Starter: «Por la presente, la abajo firmante informa que, leída la transcripción policial, ...»

concepts.grammar: Legal register and the future subjunctive (quien faltare a la verdad; si así no se hiciere; por la presente, la abajo firmante; en virtud de lo cual; adonde fueres, haz lo que vieres; di lo que oyeres); absolute constructions with a participle and its own subject (prestado el juramento; leída el acta; una vez traducida la frase; terminada la audiencia; absuelto el muchacho); language contact in Paraguayan Spanish (jopará; che ra'a; vení-na; mba'éichapa; he'i chéve; luego as an emphatic particle; aguyje); marking the source of information (ndaje; dicen que; dizque; según parece; decían en el Palacio; the mirative ¡había sido cierto!).
concepts.vocabulary: Courtroom vocabulary (juicio oral, audiencia, fiscal, testigo, acusado, acta, prueba testimonial, alegato, absolver, falso testimonio, prestar juramento, intérprete jurada) and the countryside of sugar cane (cañaveral, trapiche, lindero, rastrojo, chispa, incendio intencional).
concepts.skills: Judging how reliable each source is (police report, sworn testimony, rumour); following a planted clue from a 'irrelevant' remark to the resolution; reading legal formulas and courtroom procedure in context; understanding Guaraní words in Spanish with the help of context and glosses.

stories.title: La última palabra de Ma Petrona
stories.teaser: A linguist from San Basilio de Palenque chases the etymology of the strange word her grandmother said before she died, only to learn from her uncle that some words are not meant for dictionaries but for answering.
lines: «Resumen. El presente trabajo examina una forma léxica no documentada en los repertorios del palenquero, la lengua criolla de base española hablada en San Basilio de Palenque. Cabe la posibilidad de que se trate de un préstamo léxico del kikongo, si bien los datos disponibles no permiten descartar otras hipótesis.» Dorina Salgado releyó el párrafo en la pantalla de su oficina, en la universidad de Cartagena, y le pareció impecable y falso. No mentía en nada; simplemente callaba que la única informante había muerto tres semanas antes, que en el pueblo todos la llamaban Ma Petrona y que era su abuela. Llevaba tres semanas escribiendo y borrando aquel párrafo, y cada versión sonaba más segura que la anterior y la dejaba a ella más insegura.

“Abstract. This paper examines a lexical form not recorded in existing inventories of Palenquero, the Spanish-based creole language spoken in San Basilio de Palenque. It is possible that it is a loanword from Kikongo, although the available data do not allow other hypotheses to be ruled out.” Dorina Salgado reread the paragraph on the screen in her office at the university in Cartagena, and found it flawless and false. It didn’t lie about anything; it simply left out that the only informant had died three weeks earlier, that everyone in the village called her Ma Petrona, and that she was her grandmother. She had spent three weeks writing and deleting that paragraph, and each version sounded more confident than the last and left her less sure of herself.

Había sido una tarde de marzo, en la casa de la abuela, a dos cuadras de la plaza. Ma Petrona, que tenía noventa y un años y llevaba semanas agonizando con una lucidez que desconcertaba al médico, le pidió que sacara la grabadora: quería dejar grabados los cantos de su juventud. Cantó dos, con la voz rota, y a mitad del tercero se detuvo, buscó la mano de su nieta y dijo, con toda claridad, una sola palabra: «Kusungá». Luego cerró los ojos. La grabadora siguió encendida once minutos más, registrando el ventilador, un gallo, el llanto de las mujeres y, al fondo, ese silencio tan particular de una casa que acaba de quedarse sin dueña. Dorina tardó días en atreverse a escuchar esos once minutos.

It had happened on an afternoon in March, at her grandmother’s house, two blocks from the square. Ma Petrona, who was ninety-one and had been dying for weeks with a clarity of mind that baffled the doctor, asked her to take out the recorder: she wanted to leave the songs of her youth on tape. She sang two of them, her voice cracked, and halfway through the third she stopped, reached for her granddaughter’s hand and said, very clearly, a single word: “Kusungá.” Then she closed her eyes. The recorder stayed on for eleven more minutes, picking up the fan, a rooster, the women’s weeping and, in the background, that very particular silence of a house that has just lost its mistress. It took Dorina days to dare to listen to those eleven minutes.

En el velorio nadie supo decirle qué significaba. Su madre creyó que era el nombre de una planta; una prima, que la abuela ya deliraba. Durante el lumbalú, los cantos y bailes fúnebres con que Palenque despide a sus muertos, los tambores no la dejaron pensar, y apenas se fijó en que, ya entrada la noche, llegaron tres ancianas muy derechas del kuagro de su abuela, el grupo de edad con el que Petrona había crecido, peleado y trabajado desde niña. Las tres tocaron el ataúd y se quedaron mirándola. La mayor, Ma Cleotilde, le apretó el brazo. —¿Y tú, moná, ya contestaste? Dorina, aturdida, creyó que hablaba de los mensajes de pésame que se le acumulaban en el teléfono.

At the wake nobody could tell her what it meant. Her mother thought it was the name of a plant; a cousin, that her grandmother had already been delirious. During the lumbalú, the funeral songs and dances with which Palenque bids farewell to its dead, the drums would not let her think, and she barely noticed that, late in the night, three very upright old women arrived from her grandmother’s kuagro, the age group Petrona had grown up, quarrelled and worked with since she was a girl. The three of them touched the coffin and stood looking at her. The eldest, Ma Cleotilde, squeezed her arm.
“And you, child, have you answered yet?”
Dorina, dazed, thought she meant the condolence messages piling up on her phone.

Dorina había oído las palabras lumbalú, bullerengue y champeta mucho antes que la palabra «fonema». Se había ido de Palenque a los diecisiete años con una beca y había vuelto convertida en la primera doctora en lingüística de su familia, lo cual en Cartagena era un mérito y en Palenque, sospechaba, una forma elegante de haberse ido. En el colegio de Cartagena había aprendido a guardarse el palenquero para las llamadas a casa, y en la universidad, años después, a sacarlo de nuevo, ahora con transcripción fonética y notas al pie. A veces recordaba que, de niña, cuando se escapaba al arroyo, la abuela no la llamaba por su nombre sino con un grito largo desde la loma, y que ella volvía corriendo sin preguntarse nunca qué decía aquel grito. En su bandeja de entrada esperaba desde hacía meses un correo del rector de la escuela del pueblo, que le ofrecía una plaza de profesora de lengua palenquera dentro del programa de etnoeducación. No lo había contestado. Tal vez no lo contestara nunca; a lo mejor alguien más joven aceptaba el puesto y la sacaba del apuro.

Dorina had heard the words lumbalú, bullerengue and champeta long before she heard the word “phoneme”. She had left Palenque at seventeen on a scholarship and had come back as the first PhD in linguistics in her family, which in Cartagena was an achievement and in Palenque, she suspected, an elegant way of having left. At secondary school in Cartagena she had learned to keep Palenquero for phone calls home, and at university, years later, to bring it out again, now with phonetic transcription and footnotes. Sometimes she remembered that, as a child, when she ran off to the stream, her grandmother didn’t call her by her name but with a long shout from the hill, and that she would come running back without ever wondering what that shout said. In her inbox, for months, an email had been waiting from the head of the village school, offering her a post teaching the Palenquero language as part of the ethno-education programme. She had not answered it. Perhaps she never would; maybe someone younger would take the job and get her off the hook.

¿Qué habrá querido decir? Dorina se desvelaba haciéndose la misma pregunta. Escuchó la grabación de campo hasta gastarla: la ka inicial, la nasal antes de la ge, la última sílaba acentuada, como en moná. En el cuaderno ensayaba glosas y las tachaba. Kusungá no aparecía en ningún diccionario ni en ningún corpus, tampoco en las listas de palabras de origen africano que habían recopilado los especialistas. «Se constata la ausencia de la forma en las fuentes consultadas», escribió en el borrador. Lo que no escribió era lo que de verdad la inquietaba: que su abuela, que había hablado toda la vida para que la entendieran, hubiera elegido para morirse una palabra que nadie entendía. Ojalá le hubiera preguntado a tiempo, pensaba; ojalá alguien en el pueblo la recuerde.

What could she have meant? Dorina lay awake asking herself the same question. She played the field recording until she had nearly worn it out: the initial k, the nasal before the g, the stressed final syllable, as in moná. In her notebook she tried out glosses and crossed them out. Kusungá did not appear in any dictionary or corpus, nor in the lists of words of African origin that specialists had compiled. “The form is found to be absent from the sources consulted,” she wrote in the draft. What she didn’t write was what really troubled her: that her grandmother, who had spoken all her life so as to be understood, had chosen to die with a word nobody understood. If only she had asked her in time, she thought; let’s hope someone in the village remembers it.

Fue entonces cuando pensó en Kiese Mbemba. El lingüista congoleño, nacido cerca de Matadi y hablante de kikongo desde la cuna, pasaba un semestre en la universidad estudiando el sustrato africano del palenquero, y en los pasillos tenía fama de escuchar mucho y opinar poco. Oyó la grabación tres veces, con los ojos cerrados. —Tal vez la palabra venga del kikongo —dijo al fin—; tal vez no venga de ninguna parte. Hay raíces parecidas en mi lengua, pero parecido no es lo mismo, y usted lo sabe mejor que yo. —A lo mejor solo estaba delirando. —Quizá. Pero las palabras que se dicen al final rara vez se dicen por azar. ¿Ya le preguntó a la gente de su abuela?

That was when she thought of Kiese Mbemba. The Congolese linguist, born near Matadi and a Kikongo speaker from the cradle, was spending a semester at the university studying the African substrate of Palenquero, and in the corridors he had a reputation for listening a lot and giving few opinions. He listened to the recording three times with his eyes closed.
“Perhaps the word comes from Kikongo,” he said at last; “perhaps it comes from nowhere at all. There are similar roots in my language, but similar is not the same, and you know that better than I do.”
“Maybe she was just delirious.”
“Perhaps. But the words people say at the end are rarely said by chance. Have you asked your grandmother’s people?”

La gente de su abuela era, sobre todo, su tío Evaristo Cassiani, el hijo mayor de Petrona, sesenta y ocho años, respetado en su kuagro y en todo el pueblo, que había visto pasar por su puerta más investigadores con grabadora de los que podía contar desde que la UNESCO proclamó el espacio cultural de Palenque obra maestra del patrimonio oral e inmaterial de la humanidad, en 2005. Dorina lo llamó un domingo.
—¿Qué más, tío? Es por la palabra de la abuela.
—Ajá. ¿Y eso es pa' tu libro o pa' ti?
—Pa' las dos cosas, supongo.
—Entonces no es pa' ninguna —contestó él, y cambió de tema con esa cortesía con que en Palenque se cierra una puerta.

Her grandmother’s people were, above all, her uncle Evaristo Cassiani, Petrona’s eldest son, sixty-eight, respected in his kuagro and throughout the village, who had seen more researchers with recorders pass his door than he could count since UNESCO proclaimed the cultural space of Palenque a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, in 2005. Dorina called him one Sunday.
“How’s it going, uncle? It’s about grandma’s word.”
“Uh-huh. And is that for your book or for you?”
“For both, I suppose.”
“Then it’s for neither,” he replied, and changed the subject with that courtesy with which, in Palenque, a door is closed.

Dorina colgó furiosa. Tendría sus razones el tío, pensó, pero también ella tenía las suyas: era nieta antes que académica. ¿O sería al revés? Esa noche, en el balcón de su apartamento de Manga, se descubrió repasando, con una crueldad que no conocía en sí misma, las veces que había dicho «vuelvo en diciembre» y no había vuelto. Quizá Evaristo tenía razón. Cuando le contó la llamada a Kiese, este se encogió de hombros.
—Será su tío muy terco, pero no es tonto. No hay peor sordo que el que no quiere oír, y a veces el sordo es el que pregunta. Vamos a verlo. Hablando se entiende la gente.

Dorina hung up furious. Her uncle might have his reasons, she thought, but she had hers too: she was a granddaughter before she was an academic. Or was it the other way round? That night, on the balcony of her flat in Manga, she caught herself going over, with a cruelty she didn’t know she had, all the times she had said “I’ll be back in December” and hadn’t come back. Maybe Evaristo was right. When she told Kiese about the call, he shrugged.
“Your uncle may be very stubborn, but he’s no fool. There are none so deaf as those who will not hear, and sometimes the deaf one is the one asking the questions. Let’s go and see him. Talking is how people understand each other.”

Viajaron un sábado, en el carro de una colega, por la carretera que sale de Cartagena entre potreros y lomas. En la plaza, la estatua de Benkos Biohó, el líder cimarrón con cuyo nombre la tradición asocia la fundación del palenque, alzaba los brazos con las cadenas rotas, y unos niños jugaban a su sombra gritándose en palenquero. Kiese se detuvo a escucharlos. «Ma moná», repitió, sonriendo: en palenquero, moná es «niño», y ma marca el plural, una partícula que los especialistas relacionan con el kikongo. Dorina le explicó que el Ma de Ma Petrona era otra cosa, el trato de respeto y cariño que se da a una mujer mayor. Kiese anotó la diferencia sin decir nada, y a Dorina le pareció que su colega aprendía más callando que ella preguntando.

They travelled one Saturday, in a colleague’s car, along the road that leaves Cartagena between pastures and hills. In the square, the statue of Benkos Biohó, the maroon leader whose name tradition links to the founding of the palenque, raised its arms with broken chains, and some children were playing in its shade, shouting to each other in Palenquero. Kiese stopped to listen to them. “Ma moná,” he repeated, smiling: in Palenquero, moná means “child”, and ma marks the plural, a particle that specialists link to Kikongo. Dorina explained that the Ma in Ma Petrona was something else, the respectful, affectionate form of address given to an older woman. Kiese noted the difference without saying anything, and it seemed to Dorina that her colleague learned more by keeping quiet than she did by asking.

Encontraron a Evaristo al atardecer, sentado en una silla de madera junto a una pared encalada en la que descansaban dos tambores. No le preguntaron nada. Kiese le habló de su propio pueblo, de los nombres que allá no se dicen delante de extraños, de una abuela suya que también se había muerto diciendo algo que nadie entendió. Evaristo lo escuchó largo rato y luego miró a su sobrina. —Tú quieres saber de dónde viene la palabra. Eso no importa. Lo que importa es pa' qué sirve. Kusungá era el nombre del kuagro de tu abuela, cuando eran unas pelaítas. Cuando una se iba lejos y tardaba en volver, las otras subían a la loma y gritaban el nombre hasta que la ausente regresaba, aunque fuera años después. Eso no es una palabra, mija. Es un llamado.

They found Evaristo at dusk, sitting on a wooden chair beside a whitewashed wall with two drums leaning against it. They didn’t ask him anything. Kiese told him about his own village, about the names that are not spoken there in front of strangers, about a grandmother of his who had also died saying something nobody understood. Evaristo listened to him for a long time and then looked at his niece.
“You want to know where the word comes from. That doesn’t matter. What matters is what it’s for. Kusungá was the name of your grandmother’s kuagro, when they were little girls. When one of them went far away and was slow to come back, the others would climb the hill and shout the name until the absent one returned, even if it was years later. That’s not a word, honey. It’s a call.”

Dorina sintió que algo se le acomodaba en el pecho, como una pieza que llevaba semanas fuera de su sitio. La abuela no estaba delirando, o quizá sí, pero no al elegir la palabra. Las tres ancianas del velorio habían venido a contestar el llamado, y Ma Cleotilde le había preguntado lo único que importaba: si ella, la nieta que se había ido, pensaba contestar también. Y de pronto supo qué decía, tantos años atrás, aquel grito largo desde la loma que la hacía volver corriendo del arroyo. ¿Por qué se lo habría dicho a ella y no a sus hijos? Tal vez porque sus hijos nunca se habían ido. El tío se rió por primera vez en toda la tarde.
—El que nace pa' tamal, del cielo le caen las hojas. Tú naciste pa' esto, mija, aunque te hayas ido a buscarlo tan lejos.

Dorina felt something settle into place in her chest, like a piece that had been out of position for weeks. Her grandmother hadn’t been delirious, or perhaps she had, but not when she chose the word. The three old women at the wake had come to answer the call, and Ma Cleotilde had asked her the only thing that mattered: whether she, the granddaughter who had left, intended to answer too. And suddenly she knew what that long shout from the hill had been saying all those years ago, the one that made her come running back from the stream. Why would her grandmother have said it to her and not to her own children? Perhaps because her children had never left. Her uncle laughed for the first time that whole afternoon.
“You can’t run from what you were born for. You were born for this, honey, even if you went so far away to look for it.”

Esa noche, en la casa de la abuela, Dorina reescribió el resumen: «Los datos apuntan a un uso restringido al ámbito del kuagro, lo cual explicaría su ausencia de los repertorios publicados. Cabe señalar que la comunidad hablante considera la forma parte de un saber no destinado a la difusión». Lo leyó en voz alta, y Kiese asintió: era exacto. —Es un buen párrafo —dijo—. Tan bueno que cualquiera podría citarlo sin haber pisado nunca este pueblo. Después lo borró entero. Hay cosas, pensó, que un artículo puede describir con toda precisión y, aun así, traicionar. En lugar de enviarlo a la revista, abrió el correo del rector, que llevaba meses esperando respuesta, y escribió dos líneas: aceptaba la plaza y empezaba en enero.

That night, in her grandmother’s house, Dorina rewrote the abstract: “The data point to a use restricted to the domain of the kuagro, which would explain its absence from published inventories. It should be noted that the speech community regards the form as part of a body of knowledge not intended for dissemination.” She read it aloud, and Kiese nodded: it was accurate.
“It’s a good paragraph,” he said. “So good that anyone could quote it without ever having set foot in this village.”
Then she deleted the whole thing. There are things, she thought, that an article can describe with complete precision and still betray. Instead of sending it to the journal, she opened the head teacher’s email, which had been waiting months for an answer, and wrote two lines: she accepted the post and would start in January.

En Cartagena hubo quien dijo que tiraba su carrera por la borda; en Palenque, que la muchacha volvía por sus fueros. Dorina no discutió con nadie. La primera mañana de clases, en un aula con el ventilador dañado, escribió en el tablero «ma moná», y treinta niños se rieron de que una doctora viniera a enseñarles lo que ya sabían. Al salir, vio a Ma Cleotilde sentada en la puerta de su casa, al final de la calle. La anciana no dijo nada; solo levantó la barbilla, como quien espera. Dorina se detuvo, respiró hondo y la palabra le salió entera, con la última sílaba acentuada, igual que en la grabación:
—¡Kusungá!
Y desde la puerta, despacio, la vieja contestó.

In Cartagena there were those who said she was throwing her career away; in Palenque, that the girl was coming back to where she belonged. Dorina didn’t argue with anyone. On the first morning of classes, in a classroom with a broken fan, she wrote “ma moná” on the board, and thirty children laughed that a PhD had come to teach them what they already knew. On her way out, she saw Ma Cleotilde sitting in the doorway of her house at the end of the street. The old woman said nothing; she just lifted her chin, like someone waiting. Dorina stopped, took a deep breath and the word came out whole, with the final syllable stressed, just as on the recording:
“Kusungá!”
And from the doorway, slowly, the old woman answered.

stories.prompt: Imagine you are Dorina writing to Kiese a month after starting at the village school. In Spanish (6-8 sentences), tell him what you have learned and what you still don't know about Kusungá. Use quizá / tal vez / a lo mejor with the right mood, at least one future or conditional of conjecture (¿qué habrá...?, tendría...), and one hedged academic sentence (cabe la posibilidad de que..., los datos apuntan a...). Starter: «Querido Kiese: Tal vez te sorprenda saber que...»

concepts.grammar: Afro-Hispanic lexicon and Palenquero words in Spanish narration (moná, ma moná, kuagro, lumbalú, bullerengue, champeta, cimarrón, pelaítas); quizá, tal vez and a lo mejor with mood for degrees of certainty (tal vez la palabra venga del kikongo; a lo mejor solo estaba delirando; quizá Evaristo tenía razón; ojalá le hubiera preguntado / ojalá alguien la recuerde); the conjectural and concessive future and conditional (¿qué habrá querido decir?; tendría sus razones el tío, pero; ¿o sería al revés?; será su tío muy terco, pero no es tonto); impersonal academic hedging (cabe la posibilidad de que se trate; se constata; los datos apuntan a; lo cual explicaría; cabe señalar).
concepts.vocabulary: Linguistics and fieldwork words (lengua criolla, préstamo léxico, sustrato, raíz, glosa, informante, grabación de campo, resumen, etnoeducación) and the words of mourning and community in Palenque (velorio, lumbalú, ataúd, kuagro, cimarrón, agonizar).
concepts.skills: Reading fine shades of certainty and doubt through mood and conjecture tenses; contrasting academic prose with Caribbean colloquial speech; understanding Palenquero words from context and glosses; following a planted clue (a question at a wake, a childhood shout) to a resolution that is social, not etymological.

c2-07.topic: Legal register and the future subjunctive
c2-07.explain: Statutes, court formulas and old proverbs keep the future subjunctive (-re: faltare, hiciere, fueres, oyeres) for hypothetical conditions and open relative clauses: quien faltare = 'whoever shall fail', si así no se hiciere = 'should this not be done'. Everyday Spanish replaces it with the present subjunctive (quien falte) or the present indicative after si (si no se hace). It sits beside fixed legal formulas: por la presente, el/la abajo firmante, en virtud de, obrante en autos. English has a similar fossil in 'shall' and 'should this occur'. Learners recognise it but should not use it in normal speech or e-mails. Common error: using it for real past events or after a past main verb (*cuando se hiciere ayer).
examples: Quien faltare a la verdad en su declaración incurrirá en falso testimonio.
Whoever shall fail to tell the truth in their testimony shall be guilty of perjury.
si así no se hiciere, que se deje constancia de la omisión en el acta
should this not be done, that the omission be recorded in the minutes
y di lo que oyeres, pero di que lo oíste
and repeat what you hear, but say that you heard it

c2-07.explain: An absolute construction is a participle with its own subject, placed before the main clause to say what has just been completed: terminada la audiencia = 'once the hearing was over'. The participle agrees with its subject, not with the subject of the main verb: leída el acta (feminine, despite el), absuelto el muchacho. Una vez + participle makes the sequence explicit. It is typical of legal, procedural and literary prose; in conversation you would say cuando terminó la audiencia. English uses 'once/after + clause' or 'the hearing over'. Common error: using a gerund (*leyendo el acta) or forgetting agreement (*leído el acta).
examples: Leída el acta de la declaración policial, la presidenta preguntó a la testigo si la ratificaba.
Once the record of the police statement had been read, the presiding judge asked the witness whether she confirmed it.
Una vez traducida la frase, nadie dijo nada.
Once the sentence had been interpreted, nobody said anything.
Terminada la audiencia, el fiscal alcanzó a Perla en la escalera.
Once the hearing was over, the prosecutor caught up with Perla on the stairs.
Absuelto el muchacho, la sala se vació en pocos minutos.
Once the young man had been acquitted, the courtroom emptied in a few minutes.

c2-07.explain: Most Paraguayans are bilingual, and everyday speech (jopará) moves between Spanish and Guaraní inside a sentence. Switches are not mistakes: they signal closeness, rural or family settings, and who is being addressed. Perla greets the witness in Guaraní (mba'éichapa) and asks her question with che ra'a ('my friend') to put her at ease. Guaraní particles also enter Spanish: -na softens a request (vení-na), and luego at the end of a sentence means 'that's how it is', not 'later'. Voseo (vení, sentate, vos lo viste) is the norm. Common error: reading luego as 'later' or treating every Guaraní word as a sign of poor Spanish.
examples: Iporã, mi hija. Vení-na un ratito, sentate conmigo.
Fine, dear. Come here a moment, won't you, sit with me.
Che ra'a, ¿vos lo viste o te contaron?
My dear, did you see him or did someone tell you?
Nicasio he'i chéve. Nicasio me dijo, a la mañana, cuando fui a comprarle miel al trapiche.
Nicasio he'i chéve. Nicasio told me, in the morning, when I went to buy syrup from him at the mill.

c2-07.topic: Marking the source: dizque, ndaje, había sido
c2-07.explain: Spanish can show where information comes from. Dicen que and según parece mark hearsay; in Colombia and Mexico dizque does the same, often with doubt. Paraguayan speakers use the Guaraní particle ndaje ('so they say'), which tells the listener the speaker is not vouching for the claim. Paraguayan and Andean Spanish also use a 'mirative' pluperfect: ¡había sido cierto! means 'so it was true!', expressing surprise at something just discovered, not an earlier past. English uses 'apparently', 'supposedly', 'so it turns out'. Common error: translating a reportative as a direct statement, which turns a rumour into a fact, exactly the error in the police transcript.
examples: No decía «lo vi». Decía, como mucho, «dicen que estaba».
It did not say “I saw him.” At most, it said “they say he was there.”
dizque lo vieron con un bidón, dizque fue él
supposedly they saw him with a jerrycan, supposedly it was him
¡Había sido cierto lo de la miel!
So that business with the syrup was true!
Según parece, nadie lo vio nunca; todos lo habían oído.
As far as anyone could tell, nobody had ever seen it; everybody had heard it.

c2-08.explain: Words from Palenquero and Afro-Colombian culture appear in Spanish narration, usually explained by context rather than italics: moná ('child'), the plural particle ma (ma moná, 'children'), kuagro (age group), lumbalú (funeral songs and dances), and music genres like bullerengue and champeta. Treat them as normal vocabulary with their own grammar: ma goes before the noun and Spanish -s is not added (*ma monás). Note that Ma before a woman's name (Ma Petrona) is a different word, a respectful title for an older woman. Caribbean colloquial words (pelaítas 'little girls', mija, pa') mix with them. Common error: confusing the plural ma with the title Ma.
examples: en palenquero, moná es «niño», y ma marca el plural
in Palenquero, moná means “child”, and ma marks the plural
Dorina había oído las palabras lumbalú, bullerengue y champeta mucho antes que la palabra «fonema».
Dorina had heard the words lumbalú, bullerengue and champeta long before she heard the word “phoneme”.
Kusungá era el nombre del kuagro de tu abuela, cuando eran unas pelaítas.
Kusungá was the name of your grandmother's kuagro, when they were little girls.

c2-08.topic: Quizá, tal vez, a lo mejor: mood and certainty
c2-08.explain: Quizá and tal vez take either mood: the subjunctive makes the possibility feel more remote (tal vez la palabra venga del kikongo), the indicative makes it feel likelier or more like a statement (quizá Evaristo tenía razón). A lo mejor, by contrast, always takes the indicative (a lo mejor solo estaba delirando). Ojalá + present subjunctive is a real hope (ojalá alguien la recuerde); ojalá + pluperfect subjunctive is a regret about the past (ojalá le hubiera preguntado). English 'perhaps / maybe' does not change; Spanish lets you grade certainty with mood. Common error: *a lo mejor sea; use a lo mejor es.
examples: Tal vez la palabra venga del kikongo
Perhaps the word comes from Kikongo
A lo mejor solo estaba delirando.
Maybe she was just delirious.
Quizá Evaristo tenía razón.
Maybe Evaristo was right.
Ojalá le hubiera preguntado a tiempo, pensaba; ojalá alguien en el pueblo la recuerde.
If only she had asked her in time, she thought; let's hope someone in the village remembers it.

c2-08.topic: Concessive and conjectural future and conditional
c2-08.explain: At B2 you used the future and conditional to guess (estará en casa; serían las diez). At C2 they also carry stance in narration. The future perfect guesses about a past event from now: ¿qué habrá querido decir? = 'what could she have meant?'. The conditional does the same from a past viewpoint: ¿por qué se lo habría dicho a ella? Followed by pero, both concede a point before contradicting it: será muy terco, pero no es tonto = 'he may be stubborn, but…'; tendría sus razones, pero… = 'he may have had his reasons, but…'. English uses 'may', 'must', 'I wonder'. Common error: reading será or tendría as real future or conditional time.
examples: ¿Qué habrá querido decir?
What could she have meant?
Tendría sus razones el tío, pensó, pero también ella tenía las suyas
Her uncle might have his reasons, she thought, but she had hers too
Será su tío muy terco, pero no es tonto.
Your uncle may be very stubborn, but he's no fool.
¿Por qué se lo habría dicho a ella y no a sus hijos?
Why would her grandmother have said it to her and not to her own children?

c2-08.explain: Academic Spanish avoids yo and overstatement. It uses impersonal se (se constata, se observa), fixed hedges (cabe señalar 'it should be noted', cabe la posibilidad de que + subjunctive 'it is possible that'), data as subject (los datos apuntan a, sugieren) and the conditional to soften claims (lo cual explicaría). English academic prose does the same with 'it is possible that', 'the data suggest'. The story contrasts this prose with Dorina's family speech, where the same doubt is a lo mejor or ¿qué habrá querido decir? Common error: using the indicative after cabe la posibilidad de que (*que se trata).
examples: Cabe la posibilidad de que se trate de un préstamo léxico del kikongo
It is possible that it is a loanword from Kikongo
Se constata la ausencia de la forma en las fuentes consultadas
The form is found to be absent from the sources consulted
Los datos apuntan a un uso restringido al ámbito del kuagro, lo cual explicaría su ausencia de los repertorios publicados.
The data point to a use restricted to the domain of the kuagro, which would explain its absence from published inventories.

c2-07.topic: Legal register and the future subjunctive
c2-07.q: Complete the warning read to witnesses: «Quien ___ a la verdad en su declaración incurrirá en falso testimonio.»
options: faltara
faltare
faltó
faltará
c2-07.why: Legal formulas keep the future subjunctive (faltare) in an open, hypothetical relative clause; everyday Spanish would say quien falte.

c2-07.q: Complete: «___ el acta de la declaración policial, la presidenta preguntó a la testigo si la ratificaba.»
options: Leído
Leyendo
Leída
Habiendo leída
c2-07.why: In an absolute construction the participle agrees with its own subject, acta, which is feminine even though it takes el.

c2-07.q: In ña Gumersinda's «Vení-na un ratito, sentate conmigo», what does -na add to the command?
options: It softens the request and makes it friendlier
It puts the command in the past
It turns the command into a question
It makes the order more urgent and abrupt
c2-07.why: The Guaraní particle -na, attached to Spanish imperatives in Paraguay, softens a request, like 'won't you' or 'please'.

c2-07.topic: Marking the source: dizque, ndaje, había sido
c2-07.q: The witness said «Derlis ndaje oĩ va'ekue kokue rembe'ýpe». Which Spanish version is faithful?
options: Vi a Derlis al borde de la chacra.
Dicen que Derlis estaba al borde de la chacra.
Derlis tiene que haber estado al borde de la chacra.
Juro que Derlis estaba al borde de la chacra.
c2-07.why: Ndaje is a reportative: the speaker repeats what others say, so dicen que keeps the source; vi or juro turn hearsay into eyewitness evidence.

c2-07.topic: Legal register and the future subjunctive
c2-07.q: Which sentence uses the future subjunctive correctly in legal register?
options: Si así no se hiciere, se dejará constancia en el acta.
Si así no se hará, se dejará constancia en el acta.
Si así no se hiciere, se dejare constancia en el acta.
Cuando se hiciere ayer la lectura, el juez habló.
c2-07.why: The -re form goes only in the hypothetical si or relative clause; the main clause takes the future indicative, and it never refers to past events.

c2-07.q: Rewrite «Cuando el muchacho fue absuelto, la sala se vació» as an absolute construction.
options: Absolviendo el muchacho, la sala se vació.
Absuelto el muchacho, la sala se vació.
El muchacho absuelto, la sala lo vació.
Absuelta al muchacho, la sala se vació.
c2-07.why: Participle first, agreeing with its own subject (absuelto el muchacho), then the main clause; a gerund would wrongly make la sala the one acquitting.

c2-07.topic: Marking the source: dizque, ndaje, había sido
c2-07.q: Perla exclaims «¡Había sido cierto lo de la miel!». What does había sido express here?
options: Something that was true before but is no longer true
Surprise at a fact she has only just discovered
A rumour she still does not believe
An event that happened before another past event
c2-07.why: In Paraguayan and Andean Spanish this mirative pluperfect marks sudden discovery: 'so it was true!'.

c2-07.q: Ña Gumersinda's answer ends with a Paraguayan «luego». What does it mean in that position?
options: later, afterwards
emphasis: 'that's just how it is'
therefore, so
beforehand
c2-07.why: Under Guaraní influence, sentence-final luego in Paraguay is an emphatic particle, not the time adverb 'later'.

c2-08.q: How do you say 'the children' in Palenquero?
options: los moná
ma moná
monás
moná ma
c2-08.why: Palenquero marks the plural with the particle ma before the noun, and the noun itself does not change.

c2-08.topic: Quizá, tal vez, a lo mejor: mood and certainty
c2-08.q: Complete Dorina's reply: «A lo mejor solo ___ delirando.»
options: estuviera
estaba
estuviese
esté
c2-08.why: A lo mejor always takes the indicative, unlike quizá and tal vez.

c2-08.topic: Concessive and conjectural future and conditional
c2-08.q: Which form gives the concessive meaning 'He may be very stubborn, but he's no fool'? «___ su tío muy terco, pero no es tonto.»
options: Es
Será
Sea
Fue
c2-08.why: The future of conjecture followed by pero concedes a point (será terco) before contradicting it; es would simply state a fact.

c2-08.q: Complete the hedged sentence: «Cabe la posibilidad de que se ___ de un préstamo léxico del kikongo.»
options: trata
tratará
trate
trataba
c2-08.why: Cabe la posibilidad de que expresses possibility, so it takes the subjunctive: se trate.

c2-08.topic: Quizá, tal vez, a lo mejor: mood and certainty
options: A lo mejor alguien más joven acepta el puesto.
Quizá Evaristo tenía razón.
A lo mejor alguien más joven acepte el puesto.
Tal vez no lo conteste nunca.
c2-08.why: A lo mejor never takes the subjunctive; quizá and tal vez can take either mood.

c2-08.topic: Concessive and conjectural future and conditional
c2-08.q: In past narration, «Tendría sus razones el tío, pensó, pero también ella tenía las suyas» means:
options: Her uncle would have reasons in the future.
Her uncle may have had his reasons, but she had hers too.
Her uncle should have given his reasons.
Her uncle had to explain his reasons.
c2-08.why: Here the conditional is conjectural and concessive about the past: 'he may have had his reasons, but...'.

c2-08.q: Which sentence belongs in Dorina's abstract rather than in a conversation?
options: Yo creo que la palabra viene del kikongo, ¿sabes?
Los datos apuntan a un uso restringido al ámbito del kuagro.
A lo mejor la abuela se lo inventó, ¿no?
Mi tío dice que eso no es pa' la universidad.
c2-08.why: Academic prose is impersonal and hedged, with data as the subject (los datos apuntan a) and no yo, tags or colloquial forms.

c2-08.q: In «Ma Petrona» and «ma moná», the word ma...
options: means 'mother' in both
is the plural marker in both
is a respectful title before a name in the first, and a plural marker before a noun in the second
is a Spanish article in both
c2-08.why: The story distinguishes the title Ma before an older woman's name from the Palenquero plural particle ma.

steps.say: Buenos días. Usted es la intérprete que firmó esta nota, ¿verdad? Leída su nota, le confieso que no entiendo tanto alboroto por una palabrita.
steps.en: Good morning. You're the interpreter who signed this note, right? Having read your note, I confess I don't understand all this fuss over one little word.
r: Sí, fiscal. Esa palabrita, ndaje, cambia el valor de la prueba: indica que la testigo repite lo que oyó.
Yes, prosecutor. That little word, ndaje, changes the value of the evidence: it shows the witness is repeating what she heard.
Así es. Con todo respeto, la transcripción policial omite una partícula que no es un detalle menor.
That's right. With all due respect, the police transcript leaves out a particle that is no minor detail.

steps.say: ¿Y qué significa exactamente? Explíquemelo como si se lo explicara al tribunal.
steps.en: And what exactly does it mean? Explain it to me as if you were explaining it to the court.
r: Ndaje es una partícula reportativa del guaraní: equivale a «dicen que» o «según se dice».
Ndaje is a Guaraní reportative particle: it's equivalent to 'they say that' or 'reportedly'.
Indica que quien habla no da fe de lo que cuenta; solo transmite lo que otros dijeron.
It shows that the speaker isn't vouching for what she reports; she's only passing on what others said.

steps.say: Pero cuando el río suena, piedras trae. Si toda la compañía dice que fue Derlis, por algo será.
steps.en: But where there's smoke, there's fire. If the whole community says it was Derlis, there must be a reason.
r: Puede ser, pero un rumor no es una prueba testimonial. La testigo habla por boca de ganso.
Maybe, but a rumour isn't witness evidence. The witness is just repeating what others say.
Entonces que declaren quienes lo vieron, si los hay. Esta señora, que yo sepa, no lo vio.
Then let those who saw him testify, if there are any. This lady, as far as I know, didn't see him.
Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho, fiscal.
Saying is one thing and doing is another, prosecutor.

steps.say: Supongamos que tiene razón. ¿Qué pide usted concretamente?
steps.en: Let's suppose you're right. What exactly are you asking for?
r: Que se rectifique la traducción y, si así no se hiciere, que se deje constancia de la omisión en el acta.
That the translation be corrected and, should this not be done, that the omission be recorded in the minutes.
Que el tribunal le pregunte a la testigo, a través de mí, si lo vio o se lo contaron.
That the court ask the witness, through me, whether she saw him or was told about it.

steps.say: En su margen hay algo más: «olía a miel quemada». ¿Por qué cree que eso es relevante?
steps.en: There's something else in your margin: 'it smelled of burnt syrup'. Why do you think that's relevant?
r: Porque, si el trapiche cocinaba esa noche, la declaración del señor Leguizamón no sería exacta.
Because if the mill was boiling syrup that night, Mr Leguizamón's statement would not be accurate.
No me corresponde valorar la prueba, fiscal; solo le señalo que la transcripción omitió esa frase.
It's not my place to assess the evidence, prosecutor; I'm only pointing out that the transcript left that sentence out.

steps.say: Muy bien. Terminada la audiencia, volveremos a hablar. Y le advierto una cosa: si su palabrita no se sostiene, lo diré en mi alegato.
steps.en: Very well. Once the hearing is over, we'll talk again. And I'll warn you of one thing: if your little word doesn't hold up, I'll say so in my closing argument.

steps.say: Buenas tardes. ¿Usted es otra de esas personas que vienen con grabadora desde que la UNESCO se fijó en Palenque?
steps.en: Good afternoon. Are you another one of those people who come with a recorder ever since UNESCO took notice of Palenque?
r: No, señor. Hoy vengo sin grabadora; quería escucharlo a usted, si me lo permite.
No, sir. Today I've come without a recorder; I wanted to listen to you, if you'll allow me.
Algo así, pero esta vez no vengo a llevarme nada: vengo a preguntar con respeto.
Something like that, but this time I'm not here to take anything away: I've come to ask respectfully.

steps.say: Ajá. ¿Y qué es lo que quiere saber?
steps.en: Uh-huh. And what is it you want to know?
r: Ma Petrona dijo una palabra antes de morir, Kusungá, y Dorina no sabe qué significa.
Ma Petrona said a word before she died, Kusungá, and Dorina doesn't know what it means.
Tal vez usted sepa qué quiso decir Ma Petrona con su última palabra.
Perhaps you know what Ma Petrona meant by her last word.

steps.say: Esa palabra no es pa' la universidad. Dígame la verdad: ¿es pa' un libro o es pa' la familia?
steps.en: That word isn't for the university. Tell me the truth: is it for a book or for the family?
r: Para la familia. Si usted prefiere que no se publique, no se publicará.
For the family. If you'd rather it weren't published, it won't be.
Sería para entenderla, no para publicarla. Usted decide qué se puede contar.
It would be to understand it, not to publish it. You decide what can be told.

steps.say: Hablando se entiende la gente. Pero dígame: ¿por qué le importa tanto a usted?
steps.en: Talking is how people understand each other. But tell me: why does it matter so much to you?
r: Porque quizá esa palabra era un mensaje, y los mensajes tienen destinatario.
Because perhaps that word was a message, and messages have someone they're meant for.
Porque Dorina será muy académica, pero sigue siendo nieta, y no puede dormir.
Because Dorina may be very academic, but she's still a granddaughter, and she can't sleep.

steps.say: Kusungá era el nombre del kuagro de mi mamá. Cuando una se iba lejos, las otras gritaban el nombre desde la loma hasta que volvía. ¿Entiende ahora?
steps.en: Kusungá was the name of my mother's kuagro. When one of them went far away, the others would shout the name from the hill until she came back. Do you understand now?
r: Entonces era un llamado: Ma Petrona le pedía a Dorina que volviera.
So it was a call: Ma Petrona was asking Dorina to come back.
Entonces no hace falta buscarle la raíz en el kikongo; lo que importa es para qué sirve la palabra.
Then there's no need to look for its root in Kikongo; what matters is what the word is for.

steps.say: Eso mismo. El que nace pa' tamal, del cielo le caen las hojas. Dígale a mi sobrina que la escuela la está esperando.
steps.en: Exactly. You can't run from what you were born for. Tell my niece the school is waiting for her.

c2-07.scene: Osmar Villalba is the prosecutor in an arson trial in Asunción, Paraguay. The key witness speaks only Guaraní, and the police translation may have left out a word that turns eyewitness evidence into hearsay.

c2-08.goal: Persuade Evaristo Cassiani to share what he knows about his mother's last word, showing respect for community knowledge over academic curiosity.
c2-08.goalEs: Convence a Evaristo Cassiani de que comparta lo que sabe sobre la última palabra de su madre, mostrando respeto por el saber de la comunidad por encima de la curiosidad académica.
c2-08.opener: Buenas tardes. Usted viene de la universidad, ¿no? Por aquí ya han pasado muchos con grabadora. ¿Y qué busca usted en Palenque?
c2-08.openerEn: Good afternoon. You're from the university, aren't you? Plenty of people with recorders have come through here. And what are you looking for in Palenque?
c2-08.scene: Evaristo Cassiani is a respected elder in San Basilio de Palenque, Colombia. His mother, Ma Petrona, died saying a word nobody in the family recognised, and he is wary of researchers who come to take the village's words away.

c2-07: Guaraní and Spanish are Paraguay's official languages (Constitución Nacional 1992, art. 140) — https://axl.cefan.ulaval.ca/amsudant/paraguay-cnst-92.htm ; https://pdba.georgetown.edu/Comp/Estado/idioma.html (referenced in background only; the story says Perla works in both languages)

Ley 4251/2010 de Lenguas regulates use of both official languages in state institutions; the judiciary has a Dirección de Lingüística Judicial and holds trials in Guaraní and Spanish — https://www.bacn.gov.py/leyes-paraguayas/2895/ley-n-4251-de-lenguas-br ; https://www.pj.gov.py/notas/12648-se-desarrollo-juicio-oral-en-guarani-y-castellano-en-caacupe (background; not stated in text)

Ndaje is a Guaraní reportative particle also used in Paraguayan Spanish — https://publishup.uni-potsdam.de/files/43028/doehla_hennemann_ndaje.pdf ; https://www.staff.ncl.ac.uk/i.e.mackenzie/paraguayr.htm
Mirative/adverbial había sido in Paraguayan Spanish — https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01330685
Jopará = everyday mix of Guaraní and Spanish — https://www.hoy.com.py/especiales/2025/02/02/el-jopara-simbolo-de-la-identidad-paraguaya-que-cautiva-a-propios-y-extranos

Oral public trials under Código Procesal Penal Ley 1286/98; three-judge Tribunal de Sentencia; court-registered Guaraní interpreters sworn in at trial — https://www.bacn.gov.py/libros/205/c-digo-procesal-penal-ley-n-1286-1998-legislaci-n-paraguaya ; https://www.pj.gov.py/notas/11669-nuevas-interpretes-en-juicio-del-caso-curuguaty (story names no article numbers)
Sugar cane is grown by smallholders in Paraguarí department — https://www.ultimahora.com/canicultores-desistieron-avanzar-asuncion-n2892981
Ministerio Público = Paraguay's public prosecution service; Palacio de Justicia and the Sajonia neighbourhood are in Asunción (common knowledge, not separately sourced)
c2-08: UNESCO proclaimed the Cultural Space of Palenque de San Basilio a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005 (inscribed on the Representative List 2008) — https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/cultural-space-of-palenque-de-san-basilio-00102

Statue of Benkos Biohó, arms raised breaking chains, in Palenque's main square; tradition links him to the maroon founding — https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2024/8/11/a-dream-how-the-americas-first-free-town-took-its-independence-back ; https://www.eluniversal.com.co/regional/2025/03/19/un-viaje-a-palenque-donde-la-historia-no-se-cuenta-se-vive/
Palenquero: Spanish-based creole with Kikongo substrate; plural particle ma linked to Kikongo — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palenquero ; https://apics-online.info/surveys/48

Kuagro = age group (mutual aid, socialisation); lumbalú = funeral ritual of songs and dances — https://revistas.uninunez.edu.co/index.php/hexagonopedagogico/en/article/view/1071 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palenquero

Ethno-education programme teaches Palenquero language, history and culture at the village school — https://www.mineducacion.gov.co/1621/article-208164.html (kept general: 'la escuela del pueblo', no school name)
Kikongo is spoken around Matadi (Kongo Central, DR Congo) — common knowledge; please confirm
NOT stated (unverified): the 'about 300 African-origin words' figure from the map was left out; the text says only 'las listas de palabras de origen africano que habían recopilado los especialistas'.

c2-07: Guaraní lines need a Guaraní speaker: «Derlis ndaje oĩ va'ekue kokue rembe'ýpe, peteĩ bidón ipópe» (intended: 'Derlis, they say, was at the edge of the field with a jerrycan in his hand'); «Iporã, mi hija»; «Nicasio he'i chéve» ('Nicasio told me'); «Mba'éichapa»; «Che ra'a»; «aguyje». Check spelling (ỹ, ', nasal marks) and whether ndaje's position after the subject is natural.

Check the Paraguayan uses: «Vení-na» (hyphenated -na as in the map; some write venína), sentence-final «luego» glossed as 'así es, nomás', «compañía» for a rural community, «colectivo», «vereda», «despensa» (corner shop), «anteojos», «a la mañana».

The witness warning «Quien faltare a la verdad... incurrirá en falso testimonio» is presented as a traditional formula; Paraguay's Código Penal names the offence differently (possibly 'testimonio falso', art. 242 — I could not confirm). A native legal reader should check whether 'falso testimonio' sounds right in a Paraguayan court; the story's later use ('investigara si Nicasio había incurrido en falso testimonio') is generic.

Procedure is simplified and invented in detail (interpreter raising a note, the court allowing a direct question through her, an on-site inspection with the interpreter, prosecutor asking for acquittal in his alegato). It is plausible under an adversarial oral system but a Paraguayan lawyer should confirm nothing is wrong (e.g., 'presidenta del tribunal', 'defensora pública', 'actuarios').
Perla wonders about 'dizque' via a Colombian colleague, because dizque is not Paraguayan; this keeps the map's topic without putting dizque in Paraguayan mouths.
Names checked unique vs the 40 stories, dialogues, rename-map and map3: Casilda Duarte, Nicasio Leguizamón, Rosalba Insfrán, Gumersinda Ozorio, Toribio. (Mirna was avoided: already used.)
